utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. First of all, good morning to the interpreters, to be sure that everybody can hear me. Good morning to Prosecution counsel, to Defence counsel, and I would ask the registrar to have the accused brought into the courtroom. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Since everybody can hear, let me remind you that this is a new phase -- I am saying this for the public -- a new phase of the trial conducted by the Office of the Prosecutor against General Blaskic, and we are going to have witnesses called by the Trial Chamber. I would like to have the first witness brought in, who is General Enver Hadzihasanovic. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me, General? Can you hear the Presiding Judge? Please remain standing for a few moments. I would first like for you to tell us your name, your first name, your date and place of birth, your profession, today your residence, and then you will take an oath. After that, of course, you will sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Chairman. Thank you. I hear you very well -- Mr. President. I am Enver Hadzihasanovic, General Enver Hadzihasanovic. I was born on the 7th of July, 1950, in the municipality of Zvornik in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I work at the Defence Ministry of the army, at the Federal Defence Ministry of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I am the deputy assistant minister for chief inspection in defence matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Did you keep your rank in the army, General? Shall we continue to call you General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Where do you live? If you could tell us, that would be good. You don't have to tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted) (redacted).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like you to take an oath, and then you may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You may now be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to give you a few words of introduction. You know what the origin and the reason for your coming today is. We thank you for coming, and we would also like to thank your government which demonstrated its cooperation with the International Criminal Tribunal. You are before the International Criminal Tribunal having been called by this Trial Chamber. You are therefore one of the witnesses called pursuant to the discretionary powers of the Judges pursuant to Rule 98 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence in the trial at the International Tribunal of General Blaskic who, at the time of the facts, was a colonel, and who is present to your left. I suppose you recognise him. To your right is the Office of the Prosecutor and Defence counsel to the left. At this trial, and at a point where this trial is coming to an end, the Judges wished to hear a certain number of major witnesses who occupied important positions at the time of the facts when the General was a General in Central Bosnia. Through this summons that was given to you on the 21st of May, 1999, we asked that you concentrate on three or four themes which I will now point out to you in rapid fashion, that is, the origin and development of the situation, of the conflict, since there are two versions which are completely opposed, one to the other. We are also speaking about the organisation and structure of the forces of the army that you were the commander of, that is, its importance in respect of the HVO. You saw that there was also a third subject which has to do with all of the meetings and correspondence and discussions about organisations or non-organisations in respect of cease-fires, civilian populations, humanitarian assistance, and you saw that in your summons. There is also a fourth subject, which is the perception that you have of the accused personally and professionally. The Trial Chamber especially would like for you to provide a synthesised envision of the questions since this is a two-year trial and the Trial Chamber has already heard a great number of testimonies and read many documents both from the Prosecution and the Defence. This is why your testimony will be limited to a certain time period which is relatively -- I say "relatively" -- short so that it will be directed in the way that you want to present the facts, about an hour and a half or an hour and fifteen minutes. I think that if you have to take a little bit longer, of course, you can. Your testimony will be free. You can use notes, but you cannot make a prepared statement. If you are tired -- I know that you had an accident. If you are tired, you can ask for a break. Ordinarily, the break comes in at about 11.30. Therefore, you will begin to testify in respect of the things that were assigned to you in your summons. After that, for about an hour, hour and a half, the Prosecutor will ask you some questions, and then questions will be asked by Defence counsel, and finally, most likely, the Judges will ask you some questions as well. Please try to relax. You are before international judges, professional judges. You can speak without any hatred, without any fear, and we are expecting you to tell us about what you experienced but in a synthesised manner with all of the confidence that we expect from a witness testifying before an International Tribunal. It is a quarter after ten, and we will now begin to hear your testimony. If I interrupt you, it will only be in order to bring you back to the major themes that the Judges asked you to deal with. But unless there are a few clarifications necessary, theoretically, you will be able to speak freely. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, Mr. President. I shall try to stay within the frameworks that I have to say which you expect of me. I should like to remind you that before I came to Central Bosnia and taking over as commander of the corps, I was the chief of staff in the 1st Corps in Sarajevo, and partially, on two occasions, I was an operative in the staff of the supreme command of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army. So from that aspect, I knew of the documents that defined the defence of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina as such and the constitution and the law on defence, which underwent changes and amendments, and I was also well aware of the structure of the armed force of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time in order to wage a successful defence against the aggressor. As such, I was involved in Central Bosnia, I was included not as a corps commander -- and perhaps this is something that you're going to hear for the first time -- but I went with one more man from Central Bosnia. I was entrusted with preparing several units at brigade level to help the city of Sarajevo which was under siege, in a complete encirclement and a very difficult situation. When I say the city of Sarajevo, I mean the people of Sarajevo. The order which came from the supreme command to form a corps in the region of Bosnia-Herzegovina was not implemented in Central Bosnia, so those kinds of brigades had not been established in that way for this task to be implemented. In addition to me, four other men came with the same intention from the direction of Igman, Mount Igman, and two individuals came from the axis of Trnovo, that is from the Neretva River Valley. I wrote my report quite normally and said that I could not carry out my task because the corps had not been set up and such units had not been formed. Then I was told to set up the 3rd Corps in Central Bosnia. That was my assignment. The intention was the same, to define units which would, as soon as possible, be capacitated and organised and to assist Sarajevo, first of all, and soon after, to form and conceive units which would hold the line of the front on the front line against the aggressor. Those were the basic tasks in that period of time when I came on the scene. The principles of organisation for the BH army, I am going to give you. I just want to remind you that the law provided for the fact that the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina are made up by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Croatian Defence Council, and all other armed formations which, in the system of the chain of command, command and control, were used to defend Bosnia-Herzegovina. I can give you here excerpts because I have copied out excerpts from these provisions if that is necessary. But as we had not defined, in general terms, the status of the HVO, we adopted an amendment and a decree, having the force of law, a decree law, which defined the HVO and that it was a component part of the army, and it was a valid part of the defence system of Bosnia-Herzegovina but under a united command. Coming to Central Bosnia, the system of organisation for the units was based upon the following: We applied the principles of organisation and the establishment of an army as we had been taught at military academy. I completed the military academy in Belgrade for four years after my gymnasium, and after I spent a certain amount of time in the JNA, I also went to a staff academy which lasted for two years, as a supplementary academic course. I knew the principles well, and I had to implement them. The problem of the entire region of Bosnia-Herzegovina lay in the fact that the previous law envisaged a Yugoslav People's Army as an operative army and the system of territorial defence as units to protect an area if there should be an aggression against the former Yugoslavia. But in view of the fact that the JNA, at that moment in time, joined, that is to say, was the army of the aggressor, it remained in the territory of -- just the structure of territorial defence remained in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and when an immediate danger of war was proclaimed, territorial organisations started, according to the principles and laws. So these units of territorial defence were commanded by the wartime presidencies of the municipalities and districts and the political and economic system of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In that way, there was no united command because each unit had its own area and territory, and nobody was able to dislocate it and remove it from one region to another. In view of the fact that the law provided for the creation of an armed force in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was necessary to have this territorial principle translated into the principle of an army which was able to function and manoeuvre according to requirements and the assessments of the danger that existed and towards the axes from which the danger came, and that was precisely my task. I, at that time, for the first time, met General Blaskic. I had not met him before that. I am going to say something about him later on, and if I recall, that was the last subject matter in the summons. I formed the 3rd Corps with a lot of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Sometimes we would ask you to provide some dates, please. For example, the first time you met him, perhaps you can give us some dates. That would help us. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether I have the exact date in my other notebook, but I think we met for the first time when we toured the military factory, or perhaps it was a little earlier. But I do recall that date, and the reason was that it was the 22nd of December, and we would make jokes because that was Yugoslav People's Army Day, the 22nd of December. So we would joke about it and say, how come we were touring this factory on that particular date? At that time, those were the problems that I encountered. I had to form a corps and to set it on its feet. After I met General Blaskic, I offered him the opportunity of doing this together with me. I even ensured, and we came to my headquarters, that is to say, the command of the 3rd Corps, that was just being prepared to function as a group of professionals, of experts, people that were capable of doing certain tasks and knew how to set up units and elaborate the documents necessary, and Blaskic, Mr. Blaskic, did not promise anything on that occasion, but he said he'd think about it. From that day on, it was difficult to discuss this subject. I soon saw why, came to realise why, because I had already worked in that area, and I knew the problems that existed in the area, and that was that I was disillusioned by the fact that the Bosniaks, in some towns, had already been expelled, and they were towns in which the Serbian army, the army of the aggressor, was not even close by. I learnt about Stolac, Capljina, and Prozor at that time had already been definitely ethnically cleared because there were no Bosniaks in it at all. From the local civilian leaders, I received information that they had a certain number of Bosniaks who served to clean the streets and do auxiliary work of that kind. I never received a list of those people, I didn't ask for it either, because that was not the task of the army. That was the task of the civilian organs of power and authority, that is to say, to solve those problems in other ways. I also arrived at the time when the town of Jajce was taken control of by the aggressor, and my first, second, or third day there, I spent in Travnik, actually, where I encountered enormous columns of people who had been expelled, like what is happening in Kosovo today, something similar. I do not have any documents, but it is claimed that an agreement existed that the town of Jajce be turned over to the Serbs for some reason. Following instructions issued by the supreme command and attending what had been happening on the political arena, I know that the Vance-Owen Plan was currently being dealt with and that, in that connection, efforts were being made to create conditions to halt the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In that climate, there were three sides taking part, and I was disillusioned by that once again because I considered that the HVO and the BH army was one side and that the JNA and the extremist portion of the Serbian people in Bosnia was the other side. I know that the plan contained -- could I just refer to my notes, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It contained four major documents: the agreement on Bosnia-Herzegovina; the second document was an agreement on peace for Bosnia-Herzegovina, that was a document offered on the 30th of January already; the third document was a map for the provinces; the fourth document was an agreement on transitional solutions offered on the 25th of March, 1993. I know that these agreements were, in part, signed at different periods of time and that a point of contention was always the maps, the map for the provinces and the transitional period, and in that transitional period, the definition of military relationships. In January, in Geneva, it was also a well-known fact that all sides had signed two documents. The agreement on Bosnia-Herzegovina was one and the other was -- most of the documents related to peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Also in March, in New York, negotiations continued on the remaining documents. I know that at that time, the representatives of the Soviet Union and the United States of America were present in addition to England, France, and others. I know that there were some reinforcements. In Geneva, the HDZ leader signed, as far as I know, three documents, so it is only the document on the transition period that remained for them. The president of the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the 8th of March, signed the military document. So the pending issues remained the following: Some constitutional arrangements, the map of the provinces, and the transitional arrangements. The assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, at its meeting on the 15th of March, in its conclusions, gave its support to the negotiators in New York, as far as I can remember, because I was present at the assembly. It was also said that the Vance-Owen Plan was considered to be acceptable basically, however, with certain modifications as regards the status of Sarajevo, the protection of borders, the authority of the government at the level of all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that its implementation should be an integral part of the agreement. The Serbs held an assembly of their own, or they had some kind of meeting, and I remember that they tried to undermine the entire plan. So the New York round of negotiations -- I found this in documents -- was concluded on the 25th of March with Alija Izetbegovic's signature on the maps agreement and on the transitional arrangements agreement, and also the leader of the HDZ signed the transitional arrangements agreement, and thirdly, the leader of the SDS refused to sign the two mentioned documents. I remember that the Security Council reacted by a resolution and brought pressure to bear on the SDS leader to sign this document. They signed it but said that this was on the condition that the assembly in Pale accepted this. As far as I can remember, the assembly did not adopt this and they opted for a referendum, and the referendum did not vote in favour of this. So this document was not received as valid. I think that the main problem was in these solutions that the Croatian people, that is to say, the HDZ, as far as I can remember, they wanted to have Provinces 8 and 9 -- lest I make a mistake, could I please use the map from the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, General. If you would like to put it on our ELMO, the usher will help you, and this will also allow the public gallery to follow your presentations because this is a public hearing and you didn't ask for any other protective measures. Therefore, it would be best for you to put it onto the ELMO, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, I suggest that this be seen because I think that the core of the conflict lies in some decisions of this nature. The military plan part of the Vance-Owen Plan -- well, I'm not criticising the plan. I was not authorised then or now to criticise it. I'm just trying to adopt an analytical approach and to base my conclusions on this basis, that is to say, why the military conflict took place. First of all, the Vance-Owen Plan exclusively envisaged three provinces respectively for each majority people with a certain minority of the other people. The Bosniaks got Province 1, 5, and 9; the Croatian people, with a different minority, got Provinces 3, 8, and 10; and the Serb people, 2, 4, and 6. That is where the problem was precisely. When this was being signed, in the military part, the solution for the military was the following: That the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina exclusively, at the point when this programme is to be implemented, if it is to be adopted, that is to say, this plan, be withdrawn into Province 1; the Croatian Defence Council into Province 3; the Serb army, the army of Republika Srpska, to Provinces 2, 4, and 6; and, together, the Armija and the HVO would withdraw into Provinces 5, 6, 8, and 10. The problem was as follows: These joint parts -- I can't hear anything. I can't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: There seems to be an interpretation problem here. I didn't hear the interpretation. Is there a problem in the booth? Yes, if you would please repeat the last sentence? You were talking about the withdrawal of each of the peoples according to the Vance-Owen Plan. If you don't mind repeating that, because there was a technical problem in the booth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to this plan, the Armija and -- the Armija and the HVO should together withdraw into Provinces 5, 9, 8, and 10. Since Provinces 8 and 10, just like 3, was supposed to belong to the Croatian people, according to this plan, given that there would be certain minorities of other peoples, there was a problem here as well. If this were to be implemented, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina would have to be subordinated to the Croatian Defence Council in Provinces 8 and 10, and the law that was in force at that time, and documents speak in favour of this, that the HVO was within the composition of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I am going to show a document later on. I did not see this order, but I heard General Petkovic commenting on this order, the Croatian side had signed this plan, and an order was issued that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina would have to surrender to the HVO in this area. So I think the key problem with regard to the signature of this plan was, all the other problems that existed within this area of Central Bosnia, and as you can see, they belong to Provinces 8 and 10. I think that the HVO did not have any interest in the front lines at Province 2 and also vis-à-vis Sarajevo, and that is why some kind of systematic control began behind the front line through various points, various expulsions, various provocations of incidents with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I wanted to say another thing. I know that General Petkovic spoke in public and explained on television that, in this area, the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was supposed to surrender to the HVO because there was an order of the main staff to that effect. I haven't got this document, but I think there's also an order of Mr. Boban. I had grave problems. Many people complained about what the HVO did, starting from humanitarian organisations to civilians, because they saw, in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, some kind of a protector, and objectively we could not be that 100 per cent because we had just been organised and we were very poorly armed. Secondly, we were estimating what valid military objectives were. According to our own customs and according to international regulations, civilians were not supposed to suffer. At any rate, there was a general problem concerning civilians in Central Bosnia. As in Sarajevo in 1991, 1992, 1993, these problems came into being mainly in 1992 and they started at the end of 1992 and 1993, but they actually started at the beginning -- at the end of 1991. At that time, it was not clear to me why the area of Kiseljak took part in the blockade of the town of Sarajevo. I did not understand that. Because the only part that was not held by the Serb army was that area. There were many convoys where permission had to be sought, they were supposed to pass through that area, and also other military and logistics convoys, and many of them did not even pass through this area. I see the cause of these conflicts in the decisions made by political leaders and in relation to this plan which, in fact, was never accepted nor ever became valid, and I see a cause in the decisions made by certain persons who did not abide by the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its constitution as it was, and it was only the future and democracy that could change it. As regards the causes of the conflict between the Armija and the HVO and how they came into being, that is my view. We expected that plan to be signed, and I was au courant, and I was expecting many things. Then the conflicts broke out openly. At the end of 1992, when I came in October, I wanted many times, behind the front line, with the assistance of international organisations, to resolve problems, and these were problems that were behind the front lines and those were the problems I mentioned: the freedom of movement, humanitarian assistance, not touching civilians, et cetera. In relation to this, several meetings were held, and the HVO attended, namely, General Blaskic. I attended several such meetings, and the following issues were invariably discussed: I know that in January, an agreement was signed between the staff of the HVO and the general staff of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina to stop hostilities and also to remove checkpoints and basically to resolve these problems behind the front line and to try to organise a joint command, at least in the area of Travnik, which was supposed to be a touchstone, and joint operations were supposed to be carried out against the Serb aggressor. Many things had been agreed upon, but they were implemented with great difficulty. The reasons were probably in a lack of willingness or perhaps because such instructions were not received from higher instances. There are many details involved in these conflicts. Mr. Chairman, you said that many witnesses were heard and there are probably many documents. If I'm supposed to clarify any of this, I'm here and I'm ready to do so. I don't know if I took care of Questions 2 and 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, feel free to say what you want to say, but we would like to know in general how the conflict was carried out or what the enclaves were, what was the relationship of the forces. All through these two years, we've heard that the fighting was in the enclaves, who was besieged, who was carrying out the siege. As the 3rd Army Corps, we would like to have your feelings about that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. I don't know who explained the siege of the enclave; however, there is a valid military assessment in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that was to keep the territory and to strengthen the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to start liberation, and that is how we re-oriented ourselves in all areas in that period, including Central Bosnia. The 3rd Corps, as a corps at that time, had about 32.000 men, soldiers, and they were organised in brigades and later on in operative groups, and they were made up of people who belonged to the former structure of the Territorial Defence. Most members of the army, 80 or 90 per cent even, were oriented towards the front line against the aggressor. Those were their assignments. Bearing in mind the problems that were there previously, Stolac, Capljina, Prozor, everything I mentioned, Jajce, and also certain symptoms that had already prevailed in Central Bosnia and that were present there as well and that ended with expulsions of people, those were those problems that I mentioned: the freedom of movement, various checkpoints, controls, stopping convoys, mistreating people, and, finally, killing people or detaining people. A decision was made in respect of the danger that was coming from behind, that is to say, that such action should not be permitted to expand because these actions did not take place in the Lasva Valley when Stolac and Capljina were taking place. This happened only later successively. Our only objective was to prevent a further expansion and to create such an area so that we could communicate with the front line, towards the front line, and with the 2nd Corps, because, as regards our general assessment, when I left my post, I knew that there was a plan and I knew from earlier on that the main idea was to bring the corps together to help Sarajevo. After the order relating to Provinces 8 and 10 was not accepted, then there was a conflict between the army and the HVO, and this open conflict meant the following: stopping troops that were moving to the front line, removing them in part, detaining them in part. And then Ahmici happened. As far as I know, before April, in sections of the front, there was a smaller portion of the HVO, according to the different maps which I haven't got here with me, but as I was convinced, as I had been convinced by people, witnesses from Jajce, fighters who were there, that part of the HVO in Jajce, that the Serbian aggressor had gone into and passed through Jajce, I was afraid that this would happen in Central Bosnia where the HVO was also present, and I was right. Prior to the conflicts in April, on no part of the front line against the Serb aggressor was there a single HVO unit. They had been withdrawn. Blocking this area with a smaller portion of forces, we wanted to prevent expansion, quite simply, expansion of the conflict to engulf other regions. Nobody can claim here that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not trust the Croatian people. It did. It also trusted the HVO. It had confidence in them, but there could be no agreement, and I can ascribe to that. For the greater portion of 1991 and 1992, there were Croats within the structure of the BH army because the army was considered to be a united armed force for the defence of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I, myself, as a commander was not bothered by that. My personal driver was a Croat. My administrative worker at my headquarters, for example, a lady there, she was of Croatian ethnicity, and I had full confidence in her receiving documents, bringing me the documents, and dispatching them. She one day left me, crying. She said, "I apologise, Commander, but I have to leave. I have been threatened and been called by the HVO, both myself and my husband, and I have to leave the army," and her name, the woman's name was Ana Kurevija. She left the army, but she didn't go the HVO. She went to a third country. I think she has now returned to Bosnia. There are a series of other examples that I could quote to illustrate the situation in Central Bosnia and in the 3rd Corps zone. I think that these exclusive conclusions and the orders, military orders that followed were at the crux of the conflict, and in those conflicts, it is quite logical to say, and I know that General Blaskic was the commander in Central Bosnia, just as I was the commander in Central Bosnia. Is that enough on that topic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: In part, but only in part. We would like to know, starting with the significance of your forces in the conflict with the HVO, what was the chain of command within the HVO? Also, when the conflict broke out, did you speak with Colonel Blaskic at that time? You saw the conflict arising with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You had the impression that HVO troops or HVO soldiers were deserting the front line against the Serbs who were your common enemy. That's part of the second theme that we've asked you to speak to us about. If you could try to concentrate on that, before you speak about the cease-fires and meetings and also the crimes that were committed inter alia at Ahmici. Before you talk about that, we would like to know how, at the time that the conflict was about to become very, very serious, that is, the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993, how you saw the HVO chain of command, what were the relationships between General Blaskic and the political leaders, how the HVO command exercised its authority over the special units or the military police, and then we will take up, if you agree, the question of Ahmici and the different meetings, the cease-fires, and the organisation of humanitarian assistance. Do you agree with that? Could you concentrate on that type of question? Then if you wish to take a break, just tell us. Ordinarily, our break is around a quarter after eleven or twenty after eleven. Can you continue now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I shall continue up to that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you understood me when I said that General Blaskic and myself attended and graduated from the same schools, me perhaps at a somewhat higher level, but the principles and standards that we were taught, the chain of command was the same. Whether they were applied in the HVO, I was not able to check, but I think they were, and that is, we knew the structure of the units, and we knew in each unit the structure of command, who was the superior, who was the subordinate, who issued orders to whom, who was in command, and who received orders from whom. To put it in simpler terms, in the BH army, it was as follows: Tasks and assignments came from the main staff, the headquarters, and the headquarters was the headquarters in command of the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and orders of this kind would come down to the corps who then elaborated them, assessed them, determined the forces and the materiel, battalions, support, and so on, and everything else in line with the resources and manpower it had. Then it would issue orders downwards, what their assignments were in performing the individual tasks. I think that that was the same principle in the HVO. If a unit was given to me from other areas, from another corps, for example, then I commanded that unit up until -- as long as it was in my area and that particular task or mission was being implemented. Once this was over, it would be returned. If there was a superior command and if a superior command wanted to bring in more units to a given area and to use those units in that area, on that territory, then the rule was that that superior command should form a provisional command to command the mission in that area where the units were mixed, units from two compositions. That was done when approximately the same number of forces was being brought in as existed in the area already. Then the higher command would establish a forward command post. If the number was smaller, if it was a smaller number of forces compared to the existing number of forces already deployed in the area, then those units were placed under the command of the commander in the region, already in the region. That is what we call attachment. Those were the principles and standards that we were taught.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like you to concentrate on a very important point for the Judges, that is, once the conflict had become open between you and the HVO, from your point of view, what was the chain of command of General Blaskic in relation to what seemed to be his own hierarchy? So long as there was not an open conflict, I understand, but I would like you to help us in respect of the chain of command within the HVO. Could you say something to us about that, starting with the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise for repeating. They were the standards and principles that we were taught at school. If General Blaskic was in command in Central Bosnia, I do believe that he applied them, as I myself did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'll be more specific. The Judges, over quite a long time during this trial, at least from the Defence, received the idea, frequently supported by documents, that there were units that were not part of the direct hierarchy of General Blaskic, that is, the special units, the Vitezovi, the military police, and that these units were very frequently engaged in atrocities that were committed in that area. If you would prefer that we speak first about Ahmici, that would be fine, but we would like to have your idea on this question. You will be asked questions by the Defence and by the Prosecutor. I did not want to interrupt you, but if you prefer, I can guide you in respect of this summons that was sent to you and for which we would like to hear your point of view.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps I wasn't clear enough, but I think I was precise. If the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia had a number of soldiers, as far as I know, at the time, if they had about 21.000 soldiers and if units were brought in numbering 500 or 600 or 1.000 soldiers, doesn't matter, then the commander of the military structure numbering 21.000 is in command over that unit which has been brought in. There is no logic that he should not command them. They were the standards and principles that we were taught and applied, and it is as I say. Had there been 5.000 soldiers there and 7.000 brought in, then the logic would be that the person who had 7.000 would be in command, that is, a superior command would define that. I think that those units which were there, that Blaskic knew about them and that he should have and must have commanded them. If he did not know, let me be precise, and if he could not, then he should have undertaken measures to prevent them from doing what they did because that is what I would have done. The reason: In Central Bosnia, I had problems with a group of foreigners that they called the Mujahedin, and they came from different countries of the world. I did not want them in the army structure, but in cooperation with the Internal Affairs Ministry, we expelled them and disarmed them, and this was brought in a parallel position with the 7th Muslim Brigade. Those foreigners were never within the composition of that particular brigade, and while I was the commander, they were never within the composition of the Armija. A written document or paper, a written statement was given by me to Ambassador Thebault, the head of the European Monitoring Mission, a document to that effect. I don't know whether he has it and whether he can present it, but that is how it was, and he can confirm that. This part, referring to me and the 3rd Corps, I mention because I want to say that that or something similar should have taken place within the HVO. I could not have turned a blind eye if somebody complained to me and said that somebody from the Armija was making problems. I had to take measures to prevent that from being so. As for the military conflicts, that is another matter altogether. Those are different questions, different problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please continue, starting with the third subject that we asked you to deal with, that is, starting from April, the crimes, the atrocities that have been recognised and objectively considered to have been recognised in this trial, that is, in Ahmici and Nadioci, and in other villages. You were a major player at the time of those events. What is your feeling? What were the responsibilities in respect of the units that came into those villages? Did those villages have strategic interest? How did you experience that period, starting with the 15th of April through the 16th of April? If you could also tell us your feelings about the political pressures that were brought to bear during the preceding weeks, that is, the offensive that started on the 16th of April in the morning, early in the morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 14th of April, Mr. -- Ambassador Thebault came to my office and he asked me quite openly, "Do you know that the HVO is preparing an attack on the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?" He did not say where or how; he just asked the question that way. I said that I assumed so, that I did not know the day or date but that I did assume that this could happen very quickly. He asked me further, "How are you going to defend yourselves?" And my answer was that a commander would be mad to want two fronts. I was in a very difficult position. I did not wish that conflict to take place, but in analysing with my associates the overall situation, we could have assumed that something of that kind was going to happen, but I could not have supposed that it would be in villages between Zenica and Vitez, so far in the rear. The day before that, I had a telephone conversation which bore that out, and I can only suppose that the Court would not have accepted it because it was on a tape. But from that telephone conversation, I recognised General Blaskic's voice, the second voice I think was the voice of Dario Kordic, and the reason was because they referred to each other as Kum or best man, godfather, and people who knew them told me that they, in fact, took part in each other's marriage ceremonies and were Kum. The conversation was as follows: "You start out from the east," and I can only suppose that that meant Kiseljak, "and I will go here from Vitez and we'll march towards Zenica." I listened to that tape, and it was later published after the events in Ahmici, and it was broadcast by Radio Zenica and on Radio Sarajevo. I was not able to get the tape and I don't know whether it would be valid in a court of law, but it is convincing enough for me, that is to say, that there would be an open conflict in the region; but that it would have taken place in the way it did, I could not have even assumed that. The military directives of the BH army did not exist in any of the villages. We were armed, that is to say, we had a third of the weaponry we would have needed in 1992 and the beginning of 1993. All the weapons were always left in the trenches and in the bunkers when the shifts would change and when the soldiers would be replaced. Second, we didn't have as many barracks as we needed to house all our soldiers and the people that did not have weapons, and so a part of the people would go home to rest for a certain period of time. I did not have information, nor was it ever confirmed, that in Ahmici and the other villages, anybody who was armed and a member of the BH army was there. Possibly, when we conceived the BH army, each municipality staff received a portion of the army with a little weaponry, and they were detachments or platoons of Territorial Defence for which, by law, the wartime presidency of the municipal council had at their disposal. But I know there were none in those regions. In concrete terms, there was a Territorial Defence detachment in Zenica. First and foremost, it was in charge of defending the plateau above the Vranduk tunnel, because at that time we expected a dissent attack by the Serbian army in the area, and there was a -- had there been a helicopter attack, there would have been great problems in Central Bosnia. I don't know whether I have been sufficiently clear, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, you were clear. You can continue about the events as you experienced, starting with the 16th of April. We would appreciate your doing that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I received the news of Ahmici, naturally it was very hard for me. There was a particularly complex issue involved, and that is, the people who belonged to the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, who were soldiers and whose families were killed or wounded, particularly people from the neighbouring villages, were afraid whether they would be next. I heard about all of this through the relevant organs of authority, that is to say, the local communes, municipalities, et cetera, and the question was being put to me: "Commander, what are you going to do?" I even unwillingly went to attend a press conference to say publicly that the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina would not persecute Croats and destroy Croat villages but that it would take measures to prevent such events in the future. Part of the forces at this very complex front were set aside so that they would prevent such things from taking place further on in the other villages, and that is why this entire position was such in 1993 until the cease-fire was signed, that is to say, that the area of Busovaca and Vitez was under some kind of a siege. At that time, had anyone wanted to wage war against the HVO, various things had to be assessed. The most important thing was the following: Since the conflict had already been provoked, had we wanted to disarm the HVO, as was already done in Zenica because the HVO brigade in Zenica surrendered, they didn't want to do what the rest were doing, we had to create this buffer zone in order to prevent an escalation of further open conflicts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to go back to Ahmici. Perhaps we'll take a break now. I would like you to focus, General Hadzihasanovic, on what happened after April on the crimes, how you learned about the crimes that were committed, to tell us, in your opinion, which units were engaged in that, and how you were able to manage what happened afterwards since there were many discussions about cease-fires, and what was the impression that you received from the accused, what was the level of cooperation that you could count on, what was the role that the international organisations played as well as Ambassador Thebault and UNPROFOR commanders. That's the third subject of your testimony that was assigned to you and that the Judges asked you to testify about. All right. We'll take a 20-minute break. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can now resume the hearing. Please be seated. General, Hadzihasanovic, were you able to rest a little bit? Do you feel all right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We asked you to focus on the third subject, which is rather general, about the various meetings in which you participated, all having to do with -- excuse me. I will repeat this for the accused. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We were so used to seeing him in front of us that we have to get used to the change. Excuse me, General Blaskic. I apologise. We can now resume. We asked you to focus on the third subject of your testimony, that is, all of the meetings during which you were able to hold discussions either with the accused or his representatives about the organisation of cease-fires, the correspondence that had been exchanged; we would like to go back to Ahmici, the crimes committed there; and, lastly, all of the matter having to do with the transport of humanitarian assistance, maintenance of order, discipline within the HVO, if you have any idea about how military sanctions were organised that were taken; that is, all of the contacts that you had with the accused inter alia starting with the 16th of April. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Had there been a true intent to cooperate and had Sarajevo been the first and foremost objective -- well, I would like to give you a document that I found because it shows the chronology of events. This is a document from December. It shows that I sought cooperation so that we organise ourselves together and help Sarajevo. I got an answer that this was not possible, that talks were being awaited between Mr. Sefer and Mr. Petkovic, the 2nd of February, 1993; that is to say, that this intent was there regardless of the talks that were under way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, if the witness is going to use a document, the Defence would like to have a look at that document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. Registrar, have these documents copied, and they need to be supplied both to the Defence and to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. And this will be C3, the document that was submitted earlier this morning will be C2, and a copy has already been made and has been distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Right after the comment, I will ask the registrar to be sure that the documents are copied for both of the parties present. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first part of the document is the letter of the HVO submitting our request.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter asks for the witness's microphone to be adjusted, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "In view of the combat operations taking part around Sarajevo and in Sarajevo, it would be a good thing if we were to have you take part in active combat and --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I ask the usher to be sure that the documents provided by the witness are put on the ELMO, which will allow the interpreters to work with greater ease since these documents have not yet been distributed. Mr. Usher, please try to do that, and also position it in such a way that the document can remain -- the witness can make comments about it. But stay where you are, please, Mr. Usher, because we may still need you. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the participation of units of the HVO in combat operations, and then comes the following: "In view of the combat operations in Sarajevo and around Sarajevo, it would be a good thing if you would accept this, and we propose that you take part in active combat, and it is for that purpose that during the course of tomorrow -- the following day, that is to say, the 29th of December, 1992, you should come to the command of the 3rd Corps by 8.00 a.m." We don't have to read this. You can just have a look at it. This is just an accompanying letter of the HVO. And this is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can we ask the Presiding Judge, please, to turn his microphone off?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What is the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be C4.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The Judge's microphone needs to be turned off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says here: "In connection with your request regarding the participation of our units for offences operations at Kobiljaca, we hereby inform you that, from the main staff in Mostar we received an answer that the outcome of the Geneva talks is awaited at which Mr. Sefer and Mr. Petkovic are taking part on the 2nd of February, 1993." I kept it there, so if you don't need it, I can put it away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the chief of staff agreed, I think that on the 11th of December, General Blaskic and I met in Kakanj, I think, with the participation of international organisations, and we signed seven documents or, rather, seven orders which spell out, in precise terms, the prevention of conflicts that had already broken out. Before I came, there were conflicts in Novi Travnik, Bugojno, Travnik, Busovaca, Kiseljak, already at the beginning of 1992. We signed seven documents on the basis of this agreement, and these documents defined -- well, I'll have to be very accurate about this. The withdrawal of units from positions, this is an order that General Blaskic and I signed until the 13th of February, 1993, and in January, the agreement was reached. Then the document we both signed, the return of the population to their own homes, this is also an order for those villages where people had been expelled. Then that detained persons be released, that checkpoints be removed. These are all separate orders, so there is a document to prove each and every one of these details. Then to remove roadblocks and barricades from roads, and then the resolution of incidents, and this is defined by the establishment of commissions that are going to resolve each and every incident, smaller incident on the territory of each and every municipality. Then also an order to cover up all trenches or possibly bunkers that were dug in those areas, and an order to allow convoys with humanitarian aid and other things to pass. We signed all these documents in the presence of international organisations, and the European Monitors were there, the UNHCR, and, to the best of my recollection, the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting once again, but I noticed, from where I'm sitting, that the witness had copies of these documents. The Defence would like to have that too because he wasn't reading from his notes now. He had the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I certainly would like those documents as well, and if we could clarify, I believe the General was talking about documents dated the 13th of February, 1993. I think the transcript might have had some confusion on that, General, but if we can clarify that, I believe we are talking about a series of documents that, for the most part, are in evidence, but nevertheless, I think it would be helpful to have the General's copies as well. It was the 13th of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, once again, I would like the usher to remain near the ELMO. I don't want to have to repeat that, Mr. Usher. When a document is ready, this is a particular type of testimony, because this witness is not going to testify for three weeks, each of the parties has to have the documents in question. Registrar, if necessary, be sure that once the comment is finished being discussed, have it sent for copying, so at the beginning of the afternoon, the Prosecutor is in a position to question the witness, and then later the Defence as well. Let me remind you that the witness's time is limited, and his government asked that he not be here for several days in a row. I want things to be properly organised. Mr. Registrar, organise things that way. We would like to be sure that we understand things correctly. You are talking about the order of 13 February, 1993, are you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I asked that I read the authentic document so that I would not make a mistake, and I could have had in my own notebook only the titles of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am presenting this for the following reason: All the meetings that followed were related to these matters in terms of the subject matter that was discussed there, and whether these orders were carried out or not, who did not carry them out, why would they not carry them out. On several occasions, joint commissions were informed of this, together with international representatives, and they were supposed to have a look and see whether this was carried out or not. That is why I am presenting this, and I only read the titles of the documents. However, there's no problem. If you want me to, I can read out the entire documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Give us your comment on the carrying out of the orders, please, your comment on the carrying out of the orders.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the following meetings, until the open conflict broke out, had on their agenda these matters, the implementation of these matters, because they were not being carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I'm saying that they were not being carried out, I'm saying that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina did carry them out and the HVO did not carry them out. Because when you analyse these documents, you will see that many things were handed over to the Ministry of the Interior as regards checkpoints and other obligations and also civil defence and also the commissions that were supposed to take all of this, and these seven issues were discussed at all the subsequent meetings of the commission. The first document, conditionally speaking, the first one, this was a set of seven documents, I believe, the withdrawal of units from positions, this is an order that was signed both by General Blaskic and myself. I don't know if I have to read it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. The documents will be given to the Office of the Prosecutor and to the Defence and may be the subject of questions, but I want to say for both the Defence and the Prosecution, these are Trial Chamber witnesses testifying under a special status, and let me remind you that if you don't have time in your final conclusions, you can discuss these documents in written briefs that will be considered by the Judges. Do you have any further comments about those documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I swore that I would speak the truth. At these meetings that were attended by General Blaskic, always, or in 90 per cent of all cases, there would be a representative or a political leader, as far as I could understand this, by the name of Ignac Kostroman. He never uttered a word at any one of these meetings, but at certain points in time, because he always sat next to General Blaskic, he would whisper quite a bit into his ear, and the General took part in the meeting itself and explained certain events. At any rate, these were troublesome meetings, that is to say, once I was claiming that somebody had done something and the other side was not claiming that they had not done that, so my conclusion was that there was no will to do this. International organisations, headed by the monitors of the European Union, were always supposed to have someone present to register what had been done and whether everyone had done what they were supposed to do. That is what I wanted -- that was the reason for the presentation of these documents. Next, the return of the population to their homes. Because already in the beginning, that is to say, the beginning of January and February 1993, there were villages where the Bosniak population had left their homes, and also there were some Croats who had left their homes, but some were expelled and others fled because of their own fear, so that document also had to be defined. Their return was a complex affair because if somebody would go back, others would threaten them. With this document, we tried to define the role of the HVO and the Armija, and it was the Ministry of the Interior that was supposed to take care of security matters, at least as far as Bosnia-Herzegovina was concerned. The next document, that is the release of imprisoned and detained persons. That is also an order that all persons who were possibly brought into custody, detained, or imprisoned be released, and there are deadlines there too, but I'm not going to read the document now. Next, the removal of checkpoints. Among other things, it is these checkpoints that created the greatest problems because there was not freedom of movement, that is to say, it was fully restricted. The checkpoints were supposed to be taken over by the MUP, if they were supposed to exist and if there was supposed to be any checkpoint at all, and some were supposed to be abolished altogether. This also pertains to certain roadblocks and barricades. The next order, the problem of resolving incidents. Reference is actually made to those situations when groups or individuals would, without any orders from their superiors, create problems, and these persons had to be dealt with immediately. At certain areas, apart from the front line, there were some shelters, trenches, and foxholes, and there were orders then to remove all of this and to cover it up, fill it in, and since there were quite a few problems in terms of letting convoys pass, there was also an order as to how to ensure the freedom of movement for these convoys. All of this was done on the basis of documents that were co-signed by the commander of the general staff of the army and the chief of the main staff of the HVO, and then we translated this into orders. There were meetings that followed, about ten approximately, I cannot say for sure, and they always had to deal with the problems involved in the implementation of these matters. Then from the 15th onwards, there was a problem of the open conflict because of the order that was issued that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina should surrender to the HVO in that area, and on the basis of the law of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we could not do this and we did not want to do this, and that is why an open conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Would you now move to the point having to do with the crimes that were committed in Ahmici? When did you learn of the crimes? How were they managed or investigated by the HVO party? What were your relations with the HVO after the crimes had been committed at Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the atrocities were committed in Ahmici, I lost all contact with General Blaskic. Before, we communicated personally at official meetings -- let me correct myself. At first, this was done through personal requests and then at official meetings in the presence of international representatives, and after Ahmici, we lost contact. Perhaps an occasional fax would arrive by telephone. Whether the HVO investigated these crimes, that, I do not know because this area was now under HVO control, but I saw pictures of the crime on television, the picture that Bob Stewart sent to the world, the General, rather, the Colonel who was the commander of the battalion in Vitez, of the international forces in Vitez, of UNPROFOR. I already said that enormous pressure was being brought to bear against me, that the ordinary people were terribly upset, and I said what I said at the press conference, and they expected us to retaliate in the same way. However, the conflict spread to Gornji Vakuf, Bugojno. Our communications and help from Central Bosnia, from Zenica to Gornji Vakuf was made more difficult, so valid military objectives had to be sought and communication for the purpose of assistance. The choice made was via Guca Gora to Travnik and then from Travnik across the mountains to Gornji Vakuf, because Gornji Vakuf was held by Serb forces, so we could not pass through there. I already explained earlier on that our next objective was to contain the internal conflicts so that it would not spread further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Did Ahmici have a military interest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What information can you give us about your contacts with Colonel Stewart or Ambassador Thebault in respect of Ahmici? You no longer had any relations with General Blaskic, who was a colonel at the time, but you did have relations with the commander of the British battalion and also with Ambassador Thebault, who was responsible for the European Mission. What complaints did you have? What did you tell them? What did you demand? First of all, when did you receive information about Ahmici, and then what were your complaints that you made to Colonel Stewart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first information I received unofficially or, rather, officially on the morning of the 16th from the first people who were fleeing the area, and this information was brought to me by the head of the Civil Defence from Zenica. The municipality of Zenica and the Civil Defence had taken in the first refugees. I asked Bob Stewart to help so that at least the victims could be brought out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You spoke to Bob Stewart immediately? Are you the one who spoke to him immediately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not immediately. A few days later. As for Ambassador Thebault, I talked to him not specifically about Ahmici but about what would happen later. I told him that I would do whatever it took so that the conflict would not escalate further. After that, Ambassador Thebault was there for only a short period of time, and he was replaced by another man and I can't remember his name. I think that about two months later, the ambassador was replaced by someone else. I don't know whether this is certainly that way, but I know he left. Another problem that I asked Ambassador Thebault to deal with, and especially Mr. de la Mota, is the problem of helping people in Stari Vitez because there was a group of civilians, a large group of civilians, and they were totally encircled all the time, and the assistance sought was along the following lines: to send them food, medicines, and other things that the man in the street would need. Otherwise, in Central Bosnia, valid military objectives existed for which already, perhaps in 1991, incidents broke out and conflicts, and those were the military factories. If that can help the Trial Chamber, then I could enumerate them and perhaps locate them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Speak to us about the military targets and tell us whether you remember anything about the truck bomb. But I would like you to finish first with Ahmici. Did your intelligence services tell you more specifically who the perpetrators of the crimes committed in Ahmici were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I don't have very many details, but I do know that it was stated that this was done by the special forces of the HVO, the military police, the Jokers, I think they were, too, and the Apostles, or something of that kind, but they were special forces of the HVO, special purposes forces, because we didn't have insight into that, and the Vitezovi I think as well, something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let's go back to Vitez and Stari Vitez, the explosives factory, the factory and the truck bomb. Could you give the Judges any information about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The factory in Vitez was an explosives factory, a factory which belonged to the military industry of the former JNA. It produced all types of explosives and rocket fuel for multiple-barrel rocket launchers. Up until my arrival, I know that at the staff of the supreme command in Sarajevo, they discussed the stockpiles in the factory and how they were to be distributed once the factory had stopped producing. Perhaps, in 1992, it still functioned on a partial basis. In view of the fact that it was a factory having exclusively chemical technology, it was highly susceptible to any military procedure; but when I came to Central Bosnia, nobody from the structure of the BH army could enter it or visit it, and the explanation given was that it had ceased to function. The other military factory was Bratstvo, called Bratstvo, in Novi Travnik. That was also owned by the former Yugoslav People's Army and the army industry, and it produced the following items and weapons: guns for tanks, the T-55 type; guns for tanks, M-84; it manufactured multiple-barrel rocket launchers of the following type -- three types, that is: multiple-barrel rocket launcher with 32 barrels of a range of 10 kilometres which had to be tractored, that is to say, a vehicle, heavy-duty vehicle, was used to transport it; the same type with a 20-kilometre range whose lancer was on the outer shell of the car; and the third, Orkan, as it was called, at 50 kilometres with 12 barrels which used cassette bombs. The next thing it produced were recoilless guns, the type of guns used --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You don't have to go into all those details, General. We don't have a lot of time, and I suppose that you are very familiar with that, better than we are. So that the factories had a very important military and strategic function; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I want to say is that the conflict existed over that factory when I arrived that year. Let me enumerate some others: Bugojno produced, in a portion of it, a civilian factory produced fuses for grenades and mines, for example. Also there was the Klokoti at Bilalovac where fuel was produced, and this was a target because it was used in the process of production in producing the mechanical part of a grenade, for the welding of steel and so on and so forth. So in the area, there were a number of military targets that were of interest, and the HVO and the Armija, we thought that it belonged to us jointly, that it was joint property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please continue if you have any other comments to make. The Prosecutor and the Defence and the Judges will ask you some questions, but I would not like to ask you questions right now. But if you prefer, we can ask you questions. I would like you to ask for your interpretation and feelings about this truck bomb. Were there snipers on the Bosnia-Herzegovina side? Did you use "babies"? All of this was dealt with in this trial, General Hadzihasanovic. Could you tell us something about that? If not, the Prosecutor or the Defence will certainly ask you questions about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were attempts from one axis to help Stari Vitez, and that was also a valid military objective. We tried but did not succeed. Second, you asked whether there were any snipers. There were snipers in every unit on both sides. The question is only how much and what targets they aimed at. So there were snipers, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General, we asked you to tell us, at the end of your testimony, what perception you had, at least during the time you were in contact with him, the perception that you had of the accused with whom you worked throughout a period of time against the Serbian aggressor, and what was your perception of that same accused after the start of the conflict and after what happened, particularly in January and then in April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I shall repeat. I did not know General Blaskic previously. I met him for the first time when I came to Central Bosnia, and I have known him to the extent that we attended meetings together and had talks. His military knowledge, I don't know how far it extended. Had we worked together at the front line, then perhaps I would have been aware of his and he would have known mine. But I was not clear why everything that had been done under the command of the Operative Zone of the HVO in Central Bosnia, behind the front line, why that was being done. I have presented my assessments. The reason for the situation and who issued the orders, I'm sure General Blaskic has said or will say. I cannot claim anything because I was not present anywhere nor did I hear anybody issue orders to Blaskic, but I do know that that kind of thing did happen, and we suffered the consequences, those of us from the Armija and the ordinary man in the street, ordinary people. That is how much I know about Mr. Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Your testimony is now complete. Let me turn to the Prosecutor. We'll stop at 1.00. Mr. Prosecutor, you can begin to ask questions, if you have any you want to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, one or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You don't have six weeks to do so, let me remind you of that, and I'll also remind Mr. Hayman of the same thing. We heard Generals who testified here for six weeks. I'm not talking about General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Be brief, and I will ask Mr. Hadzihasanovic to answer succinctly when he's asked questions. When the questions are asked, look at the person who is asking them, but when you give your answer, please face the Judges. Very well, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Kehoe:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, General. You and I have met before, and welcome to The Hague, sir. General, I would like to go back with you just for a little bit and talk to you a little bit about some of the things that were happening when you were in Sarajevo when you first joined the Armija and when it was being turned from the TO to the Armija, so we have that time frame in 1992. Let's go back to that time frame, General, and during this time frame, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the HVO was being formed; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me be as brief as possible. Yes, they were being formed. Do you need an explanation? I can give it if you do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if you could, General, and can you give the Tribunal the benefit of your views as to what the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was attempting to do, what they were attempting to accomplish.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I personally think, following the political scene at the time, because I gave a lot of thought to myself and what I thought and to my state, my country, and Bosnia, as I saw it, so let me say briefly the following: There were people who wanted Bosnia and there were those who loved it. Those who wanted it formed different types of associations, military powers, to ensure that Bosnia would belong to someone else, and I think that that was Herceg-Bosna because it did not exist in the structure of state organisations and the legal laws that existed in Bosnia-Herzegovina which had, in fact, been internationally recognised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, can you be more specific? I mean, who did Herceg-Bosna want to belong to?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: There were assessments, that is to say, that Herceg-Bosna could belong to the Croatian people in Herceg-Bosna and the community there and probably a referendum at some time in the future and to become a part of the State of Croatia. That is my assessment, my evaluation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, you talked to us a little bit about your knowledge of events in the Kiseljak area when you were in Sarajevo, and while you were not in Kiseljak, I would like to talk to you a little bit about what was happening in Kiseljak in mid 1992 when you were in Sarajevo. Could you tell us, and tell the Judges, what the HVO was doing and whether or not Blaskic was the commander at that time in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I was in the main staff of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the general staff, and I dealt with operations, that is to say, I helped devise plans to stop the aggression on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I know that information arrived about the problems in Kiseljak, and that is when I heard about the name and surname of Tihomir Blaskic for the first time because Vahid Karavelic, the present general who had gone to military academy with him, had known him and he said "I know the man. I went to school with him." The commander of the HVO in Kiseljak at the time was Mr. Blaskic; I don't know if he had a rank or not. I know that it was a problem, that the HVO had surrounded the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence and asked them to surrender and to give up their weapons, and I think that was done at the time. I did not have any influence as an operations man on the process of decision making and reactions that followed, but I do know that because I was present when that was discussed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, were you receiving information as to what was happening with the Bosnian Muslim population in the Kiseljak municipality when Blaskic was the commander?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The population was expelled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, did you learn at a certain point that Blaskic was promoted to the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone? Without giving us a date, did you learn that that event took place?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the date because when I came to Central Bosnia, Blaskic was already the commander in Central Bosnia, and because he was successful in his work, he was probably promoted to a bigger assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, motion to strike the prior answer. If the witness doesn't know when the accused left Kiseljak, then he doesn't know whether he was the commander in Kiseljak when "the population was expelled."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, counsel can draw any conclusions he wants in argument or ask questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could you explain what you mean, Mr. Hayman? I didn't really understand what you just said. You're saying there's an error in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'm asking the Court to strike the prior answer of the witness because, in this most recent answer, he has demonstrated or admitted he doesn't have a foundation for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You can argue that at the appropriate time, but let the witness answer as he chooses. Please continue, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, when you say "the reasons for his promotion," could you elaborate that a little bit and share with the Judges why you think Blaskic was promoted from Kiseljak to take over control of the entire Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I think because he had done his previous work well. Usually, you are promoted for good work. Now, whether it was good work, I don't know. I leave that -- not for me. Perhaps for somebody else it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, you noted for us that you came to the Central Bosnian Operative Zone to form 3 Corps, I believe you said, sometime in October or early November of 1992; is that accurate? Again, we're not talking about an -- just an approximation, General, would be satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, and I can tell you the exact date. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you gave us some view to this, but could you give us a little bit more detail on the state of the military affairs within the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time that you took over, with regard to weaponry, ammunition, combat readiness of your troops, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me start with the following details: Before the war broke out, the former JNA ordered that the weapons belonging to the Territorial Defence be handed in to the barracks of the JNA, and the warehouses were on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they were, for the most part, empty. When, by a decision of the presidency -- when the presidency made its decision to proclaim a state of war, that is to say, the imminent danger of war and the proclamation of the Territorial Defence as the legitimate force for the defence of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was very little weaponry because all the stores had been depleted. What existed at the beginning was scant. If I were to give you a percentage, it might have been ten per cent of the overall amount that existed. Once again, everything depended on the area concerned within Bosnia-Herzegovina.
