The Territorial Defence, in 1992, did get some weapons when the barracks of the JNA were emptied, and the weapons that were seized on those occasions went up to, say, 20, 30 per cent, and we also got some from other sides, by seizing weapons, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, would you give us an approximate percentage of how many of your soldiers actually had weapons? I'm talking about the time frame when you were formulating 3 Corps.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, up to a third, at maximum. If the brigade had 1.200 men, perhaps there were 400 rifles, or 1.500 at maximum, although not everybody had that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you the same question, General, as we move into 1993 and the events that took place in 1993. What was your status of weaponry within the brigades going through 1993? Was it the same? Was it different? Did it improve? Did it get worse? Can you give the Judges an idea about that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: The situation was the worst in 1993. There were no improvements then, so there was a status quo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, we were talking about weaponry. Let's talk a little bit about ammunition. What were your ammunition stores like at that time, in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't have any ammunition stores. If there were any anywhere, they were very poor. I know that my men at the front line asked for cigarettes and bullets, and they were satisfied with that too. I know there were some with ten bullets, up to 30 at maximum, that is to say, one clip per rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these soldiers that you had on the front line, tell us a little bit about the front line. Who was this front line against and how long a front line was this, how many kilometres?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: The front line that I talked about related to the aggressor, and there's another thing I did not say in respect of the front line before with regard to the 1st Corps and the 2nd Corps, and that was 500 to 600 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The aggressor that you're talking about are the Serbs, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of this front line that you are covering, between 500 to 600 kilometres, how much of that front line was the Armija covering and how much was the HVO covering?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: In percentage terms, I mean, I only know the area, so let me not make a mistake, there was very little. There was the area around Zepce, the area towards Gornji Vakuf, and then the rest was outside my own zone. There was the Neretva Valley, I don't know if that was part of the area facing the Serbs, and then there was the area in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us concentrate, General, on the area that you know about, which is the area covered by 3 Corps. Again, give us the amount of front line you were covering, how much you were covering, and how much the HVO was covering on that front line against the VRS?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be sufficient if I gave you percentage terms? I cannot recall the numbers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine, General. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if it was ten per cent, but before the conflict, it wasn't even a kilometre, in April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let us talk about the series of conflicts that came up, General, after you became the commander of 3 Corps in October and November of 1992. You had a conflict in Gornji Vakuf that commenced in January of 1993; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. It started in January, but it escalated in June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk first about the January conflict, and give the Court your views as to what that conflict was all about, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: In that conflict, I think that what was needed was to create incidents to keep the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina busy, and then the decision was awaited in respect of the Vance-Owen Plan, and then it would be thrown onto its knees, and then it would no longer exist. That was the end of January. However, the conflict escalated in June, and I am linking this to what was happening in the area of Mostar and in the Lasva area. Finally and definitely, Gornji Vakuf had to be seized, but in Lasva, problems were supposed to be created so that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina could not intervene from Central Bosnia, from Zenica. That was the military assessment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk first about January of 1993, and I'd like to show you a report, General, that I believe you authored on the 17th of January, 1993, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have another couple of copies for the booths which may make life more easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Usher, would you give copies to the booths, please? The Judges have decided that the exhibits that were presented by the witness to the Prosecution or the Defence would be marked as Prosecution or Defence Exhibits. We are not going to set up a third set of numbering, except for documents directly produced by the witness. Is this a Prosecution document?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, this is Prosecution Exhibit 731, 731A for the English version, and I could point out that the copies of the exhibits provided by the witness have been copied and will be distributed shortly, and there are 11 of them up to this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do the booths have the documents? Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm just waiting for the witness to get the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Usher, please put a copy on the ELMO so that the public can see it. This is a public hearing. Thank you very much. Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, this is a document that you authored concerning the negotiations for the resolution of a conflict in Gornji Vakuf. The report is dated the 17th, and the negotiations took place on the 16th. If we might read through this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we might read through this, as it's not in French, Mr. President. We only have an English copy and an B/C/S copy. This is a report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You seem surprised, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I'm not surprised. I deeply apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You caught me, Judge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a report for the attention of the chiefs of the supreme command of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina armed forces. "During the night of 15/16 January there was intermittent artillery fire although less intense than the previous day. The surrounding Muslim villages of Voljevac, Here and Pridvorci were shelled with heavy artillery. These places were shelled because the movement of our troops towards Crni Vrh (trig point 1303) had allegedly been detected. The shelling of the city was somewhat less intense than during the preceding two days, although it intensified as night fell. "Around 1730 hours the HVO representatives, colonels Miro Andric and Zeljko Siljeg, arrived. The preceding night at around 2200 hours they had gone to Prozor for consultations with General Slobodan Praljak. They were accompanied by Mr. Ivica Lucic from the Information Bureau of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna (we learned his real name once the talks were over, outside the building; when the talks started, he introduced himself as Mirko Radic). During the meeting they set forth an explicit position with the demands they wanted to be carried out, as described below: - The HVO decision on the organisation of provinces is a temporary decision based on reciprocity; - If there are changes in the final agreement in Geneva, the Croats will abide by them; - The HVO forces explicitly demand that the Armed Forces: - withdraw units towards the villages; - return all units to the places from which they set out (this refers to the units from Jajce); - The HVO guarantees that it will do nothing against Muslim soldiers or civilians who have not perpetrated war crimes; - Equality will be respected in all areas, although the Armed Forces must be subordinated to the HVO and their direct commander will be the HVO commander; - Abandon the trenches, especially the repeater, and fill them in; - The Army can no longer be commanded or influenced through Topcic, Agic and Prijic; - They are willing to accept a commander designated by Commander Merdan, and who will be subordinated to the HVO in his command capacity; - Establish a joint checkpoint, with a proportional number of Muslims and Croats. It is also necessary to determine a specific number of military policemen from both sides; - All militant units should be withdrawn to villages, and the town of Gornji Vakuf must not have a single soldier with long weapons with the exception of a mixed military police patrol; - They demand a denial over the radio that they have torched mosques, massacred civilians and soldiers and killed civilians. It should also be added that a civilian was killed, the driver of an ambulance wounded, a soldier butchered and another soldier killed as he was assisting in carrying the wounded soldier into the ambulance. - Unless these requirements are carried out, they shall not be responsible for any consequences of a refusal to meet these demands, which are intended to lessen tension, halt the conflict and introduce law and order in the area in which disturbances have emerged. "This envisages that everything must be completed by tomorrow. If it is clear that these demands will not be carried out by tomorrow at around 2400 hours, or if there is no desire to carry them out, they will not wait for the following day. If the will exists, the demands are carried out and they are duly informed, they will check, with UNPROFOR mediation if they are willing, whether everything has been completed, the units withdrawn and the trenches filled. The borders are closed and the Army is already prepared to move. The borders will not be opened for anything until the problem is resolved. "When I pointed out that I was not authorised to resolve all the requirements set forth and that I needed to receive the necessary instructions and directions, I was told to transmit the requirements by packet communications to the superior command for a reply. We were warned that the death of a single Croat in the meantime could cause the deadline for the execution of requirements to be shortened. "In the part of the texts relating to the influence on the Army, the reference is to Abdulah Topcic, President of the Party of Democratic Action for Gornji Vakuf and Deputy in the BH Assembly, Fahrudin Agic, Commander of the Gornji Vakuf Municipal Defence Headquarters, and Hanefija Prijic - Paraga, Commander of the Military Police unit. "Irrespective of their interpretation that these demands do not represent an ultimatum but a categorical position, I consider the demand an ultimatum and believe they are prepared to use force if we do not accept their demands, since they have already grouped their forces from the direction of Prozor and have carried out preparatory combat activities on this axis. "During the day two civilians were killed in the Pridvorci village. The Army suffered no losses. There was extensive material damage. "Kindly reply IMMEDIATELY regarding the demands; we would then transmit the reply to the HVO representatives. "Kindly inform the President of Bosnia-Herzegovina and President Izetbegovic of these demands through the competent organ. We also suggest that the demands be broadcast, as necessary, in the media and especially over BH Radio and Television." Now, General, do you recall this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were these particular demands given to you by Colonels Andric and Siljeg?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: In the territory of Gornji Vakuf at that time, after the agreement, there was a commission for resolving incident situations. On behalf of the 3rd Corps, Mr. Merdan worked in this commission. As the head and representative of the Armija in that commission, he sent this information; and the points that you quoted, that are marked by a dash, those were the requests of the HVO, and I only sent this information further on to the general staff in Sarajevo, and I ordered in another document, which I haven't got here, that the commission continue their work and try to prevent incident situations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did Merdan inform you that he was told that Andric and Siljeg had been consulting with General Praljak during the course of these events?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he wrote.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this time, General, did you know that General Praljak was a General in the army of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not know that. I found out later. At that time, no, not in January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know at this time that Colonel Andric was an officer in the army of the Republic of Croatia at this time?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I am talking about January. At that time, I didn't know, but I found out later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, did you abide by this ultimatum or did fighting continue in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: We did not abide by this ultimatum. The fighting continued, first, of lesser intensity and then, I don't know the exact date, I think it was the 26th or 27th of June, there was full intensity with regard to these attacks, and there was a conflict going on non-stop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, my time is limited, so I'm going to shift topics a bit, and I'm going to move ahead chronologically but I'm going to move to a different topic, and the topic that I'd like to talk to you about just briefly -- and we will come back to combat activities -- but one topic that I want to discuss with you that follows chronologically is your comments to the Chamber about Blaskic being in attendance at meetings with Ignac Kostroman who, you noted for us, sat next to Blaskic and whispered in his ear from time to time. And I would like to show you a document, yet another report of yours, General, from the 1st of February of 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Prosecution Exhibit 732, 732A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, take a look at this. We are not going to read this whole document. This is a document that reflects minutes, if you will, of a meeting that you attended on the 1st of February, 1993, a meeting that was chaired by General Morillon and also by Mr. Fleming of ECMM. Do you recall this document, General, or this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, in the sequence of individuals in this meeting, number 9, of course, is the accused in attendance, Colonel Blaskic, and number 10 is Ignac Kostroman, the general secretary of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Is that the man that you were talking about that attended these meetings with Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I talked about him here, I did not remember -- I did not mention this exact title, but I said that he was a leader of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, General. And, General, at how many meetings that you attended with Blaskic was Kostroman in attendance with Blaskic? How often?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Almost all that I attended. I don't know, perhaps one or two, but mostly all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, based on your knowledge in the area, what was Blaskic's relationship with these political leaders? Was he in opposition with them? Did he seem to agree with them? Did he say anything to oppose some of their nationalistic views? What's your assessment of the situation, General, if you could tell the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I can present my conclusion on the basis of a specific event because I did not have an opportunity to communicate with the political leaders of the HDZ, that is to say, with the leaders. This was in 1993, when I was invited as a guest to the HVO staff in Vitez and this was at Christmastime. That's when I saw Dario Kordic as well, when I saw Ignac. That is the first time I saw Praljak too. According to what was said while they were extending Christmas greetings, it was obvious that they had a close relationship, close relationships. I spent only a short time there. I thought that I was supposed to attend as a guest, but I spent only a short time there. I didn't listen to all the talks. But in the greetings they extended, they only spoke about Croatia, about the Croatian people, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "they had close relationships," General, could you be specific? Who are you talking about had close relationships? Who are the individuals you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: The ones I saw there and then. I repeat, Ignac, Dario Kordic, Praljak; and I cannot remember, there were some other people there too. But these others were at municipal level, whereas these were representatives who, on the occasion of this holiday, sat at the top of the table, and that is where Blaskic was too; that is to say, at the head table, and then the other guests sat elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Blaskic was there as well?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: He was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, you noted this was -- was this Christmas 1992 or Christmas 1993?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: '93, because in '92, I was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if you -- that's fine, General. Was it after you took over as your 3rd Corps commander that this took place?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm about to go into another topic. It is 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We'll resume at 2.30, and you have about an hour, an hour and fifteen minutes left; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. The court stands adjourned and will resume at 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume the hearing. Please be seated. Mr. Prosecutor, we decided that you would have until about a quarter after three -- twenty after three, about twenty-five after three, of course, unless you finish earlier. Then the Defence will have about one hour and twenty minutes, and counting the breaks, we will finish with the Judges' questions which will take about 30 minutes. Without any further ado, I now ask you to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General. General, I would like to ask you a couple of questions about some of the things you said this morning, in particular, how they bear on the outbreak of the conflict in the Lasva Valley as of the 16th of April, 1993. Now, you talked to us about the conversation that you had with Ambassador Thebault where you noted that you didn't want to open up a second front. Can you tell the Judges, why was it not in your interest to open up a second front? Can you explain that to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, it would be normal to have responded in this way. The first and primary reason was that we, indeed, did not want the second front. The second front, even if somebody had forced us to open it, we again feared it. We did not want it because we did not have enough to open it up, and when I say "not enough," I mean not enough ammunition or materiel. But I think that what we were involved in was the pure, physical protection, and the second front would not have been right for us for this very reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in your opinion, as an officer and as the commander of 3rd Corps, what would have been the result in your line of defence against the Serbs had you decided to open up a second front against the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I have the question, please, repeated because I did not understand whether this was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Would you rephrase your question, please, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Certainly. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, as a military man and as the commander of the 3rd Corps, in your opinion, what would have been the result or the effect in your front line against the Serbs if you had -- if you had -- decided to open up a front against the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, first of all, there was no decision to open up the second front. Second, our objective was to hold the front line against the Serbs at the time, in other words, maintain it, stop losing more territory, and regroup the army so that in the future, it would be able to engage in liberation operations, and had it happened in '94 -- what did then happen in '94 and '95, this would have been different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this period of time, General, April of 1993, were conflicts and major conflicts taking place between the Armija and the VRS in Eastern Bosnia, and by that I mean Srebrenica and some of the other enclaves in Eastern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I have no detailed information on Eastern Bosnia, but there were conflicts in Central Bosnia, but they were of lesser intensity. Our assessment was that there probably were some agreements between the HVO and the Serb forces in order not to move from the lines which they had kept. These were our estimates. But as far as Eastern Bosnia is concerned, I could not really tell you because I did not follow that situation as much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine, General. I would like to show you a series of your reports, if I can, Mr. Registrar, and this is a series of reports from the 3 Corps headquarters, your regular combat reports, General, and the series I have, Mr. President, are April 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, and 16 of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your permission, I'm not going to go through these documents, as I went through the documents this morning. I would like to show the witness all of these documents at once and ask one general question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I want to say that we absolutely agree with you. Had you not said that, we would have asked you to do it that way. These are documents from General Hadzihasanovic himself. He merely has to identify them, say that he recognises them, and then you would get to the central point, and if necessary, the Defence, once it's read them, can make comments it chooses to. Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: These are documents 733, 734, 735, 736, 737, 738, and 739 for the Prosecution, and the English version has an "A."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are you going to start with 733, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I'm just going to have the witness take a quick look at all of them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. It's a set. He can look at them as a set.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Does the Defence have all these documents? No, it doesn't, and it has to be able to question the witness, so the documents have to be provided to it immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Usher. I would like to show the witness all of them at once, from 733 to 739. I just think this will move more expeditiously, Mr. President, if he just looks at all of them, and we can ask the General questions and move from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you remember these documents, General Hadzihasanovic? Do you remember them all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, the witness remembers them. Now that the witness has all of the documents, and the Defence does as well, you can ask your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can just take one more moment to just allow the witness to just take a quick look at the balance of the document, it's not going to take long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. All right. That will also give the Defence the chance to have a quick look at them also. Have you been able to look at them, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, just a little background concerning these documents. What are these documents?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: These are regular daily combat reports which were the practice in the BH army, and every unit in the BH army had to have one sent to its superior command within 24 hours. In some of these documents, there is my signature; in some, there is not. This is not essential, but sometimes my chief of staff signed some because the commander sometimes is not around, but these are the type of documents that have been produced by my command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was just waiting for the translation, General. General, are these documents based on information that you learned yourself and that you learned from others?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: These documents are based on the reports of the subordinate units which were compiled throughout the area of responsibility in the course of the day, and then the essential information is then reduced to these reports, and individual units then gather information in different ways from its own members, by reconnaissance and monitoring and by reporting and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in these reports, which date from the 10th of April, 1993 to the all important day of the 16th of April, 1993, is there anything in any of these reports that reflect that the Armija is preparing offensive operations against the HVO? Is there anything to reflect that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: It is certain that there are no such things in these documents because the army did not prepare for any such events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, on the 16th of April, 1993, who commenced offensive operations: the HVO or the Armija?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: It was the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: The beginning was in the village of Ahmici in the early morning hours. I don't know exactly -- I don't remember exactly when, about 4.00, 5.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I would like to show you a document that has been admitted into evidence and was signed by the defendant, Colonel Blaskic. Mr. Registrar, I'm looking for 456, Prosecutor's 456/100.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me remind you that these exhibits should be prepared before the hearing begins. We're wasting some time here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is my fault, it's not the registrar's fault. However ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me remind you that you have already done this. This is a recurrent misdemeanour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: However, the good news is, Judge, the good news is I am almost through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, of course, we're delighted, but you do have time if you want to ask any further questions, which will have nothing to do with the time given to the Defence. We're not using the same system for testifying as we did previously. Four fifty-six, that is a Prosecution Exhibit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Defence? Defence or Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Prosecution. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just for the record, if I'm not mistaken, Mr. Nobilo, I do believe the Defence admitted this document as well under a Defence Exhibit, but I'm not positive. Nevertheless, we can just use it as a Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, this is a document signed by the defendant, sent to your headquarters, 3rd Corps headquarters, on the secession of attack operations. The opening line of this says: "This morning your forces launched an attack on the Central Bosnia Operative Zone Command. We are surprised and outraged by such an act, on top of everything else that your members have recently done." General, is that true? Is what Blaskic is writing in this on the morning of the 16th of April, 1993, true?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why is it not true, General?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Because it wasn't so, and there are other similar documents in that regard as well as media appearances, both in television and radio, which were launched by the HVO as propaganda on the eve of the attack. Our judgement was that this was all done to justify the event which was then committed by the HVO on the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let me show you another document, which is a letter that you sent on the 19th of April to Monsignor Puljic, and once again, I do have several for the booth.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Prosecution 740, Prosecution Exhibit 740, and 740A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do the interpreters have the documents? Very well. You can proceed now, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, this is a letter dated the 19th of April, 1993, that you sent to Monsignor Vinko Puljic. Do you remember this letter, sir?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is the last document we have, we are almost through, and we would like to read this document. It is a significant document and by the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is your absolute right, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please proceed. Are the booths ready? Is the document on the ELMO so that the public can follow? Mr. Usher, is it on the ELMO? Very well. Let's proceed. Go ahead, please, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a letter sent on the 19th of April, 1993, to Monsignor Vinko Puljic, the Archbishop of Bosnia, by the witness, Commander Enver Hadzihasanovic. "We are witnessing these days in Central Bosnia and in Herzegovina further armed conflicts with tragic consequences between HVO and BH Army units. We turn to you as a leader of the Croatian people and someone in whom we believe, whose many previous comments about Bosnia and Herzegovina as our only homeland and the possibility of living here together we fully support. We call upon you to use all of your authority to prevent the rupturing of the centuries-old ties between Muslims and Croats. "The HVO leaders in Central Bosnia and proponents of an extremist policy, Kordic, Blaskic, Kostroman, Valenta, Sliskovic and Sakic, all want to leave the impression at home and abroad of being civilised people who are prepared to compromise while secretly preparing and encouraging their units to instigate terror, conflict and civil war with unpredictable consequences for the Croatian and Muslim peoples. They want to declare these territories, which have been Bosnian for centuries, as Croatian territories, because they believe that the time has come to realise this idea, which so far they have been skilfully hidden behind a smokescreen of verbal support for a united, independent and sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina. "While the HVO leaders are declaring their support for an agreement and a peaceful solution of all problems between the BH Army and the HVO, on the ground the HVO is actually pursuing a policy of force, constantly attacking and harassing the Muslim population. "All previous efforts to overcome the misunderstandings have failed due to this kind of conduct by the HVO leaders. The BH Army units have always been tricked. Their members have a very difficult time explaining why they negotiate at all when obligations agreed to in writing are usually never complied with in practice, which is entirely the fault of the HVO and their leaders. "The open aggression of the HVO against parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina has been continued these days with the most brutal and heinous means, whose application is most clearly seen in Vitez and the surrounding villages. "In the village of Ahmici on 16 April 1993, HVO soldiers committed an unprecedented massacre. They killed all human beings who were in the houses, including even children in their cradles. According to statements of eyewitnesses who managed to escape by running away, about 200 people, including women and children, were killed. We would mention that this behaviour of the HVO soldiers was unnecessary as there were no military formations in the village and no resistance was offered. "Many Muslims from Vitez, Busovaca and Novi Travnik have had similar experiences, but so have Croats who disagreed with this policy of genocide committed against people solely because they are of a different ethnic and religious background. "In this situation and in order to push the Croatian people into committing new crimes, the HVO leaders /illegible/ the BH Army and the Muslim people in Central Bosnia. "No one from the Croatian people has given the HVO leaders authority for such destructive conduct, the goal of which is to spread distrust and to stir up hatred between the two peoples, for which they will be held responsible before history and above all before their own Croatian people. "Deeply convinced that this is not a policy of the Croatian people, but rather of extremist leaders, we once again appeal to you on behalf of the Croatian and Muslim peoples to use your authority as soon as possible to try to prevent the widening of the artificially created gap between them. "Not doubting for a moment that you will as soon as possible prevent the catastrophe which has clouded relations between Muslims and Croats, we gratefully invite you on this occasion to visit the Command of the 3rd Corps, where you will always be more than welcome." Signed Commander Enver Hadzihasanovic. General, do you still stand by these statements that you wrote in this letter on the 19th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I might have one moment? Mr. President, I have no further questions of this witness. General, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. It's 3.00. We will apply an objective rule for the Defence. If it wants to use its hour and twenty minutes, it can. Would you prefer that we take a ten-minute break, Mr. Hayman or Mr. Nobilo? We don't have a great deal of time, so we won't take longer than ten-minute breaks, but just long enough in order for you to become familiar with all of the documents that were given to you. But you will only have an hour and twenty minutes. That will also allow the Judges to ask questions. All right. We will resume at ten after three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Please be seated. Mr. Nobilo, will it be you or Mr. Hayman? Mr. Nobilo, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I will be asking the questions, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Nobilo:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Hadzihasanovic, good afternoon. You probably know that we are the Defence counsel for General Blaskic, my colleague, Mr. Russell Hayman and myself, Anto Nobilo. In keeping with the Rules of the Tribunal, I should also like to ask you a few questions, as did my learned friend, the Prosecutor, before me. Let us go back to the beginning of your testimony. Can you tell us, before you came to Central Bosnia, where were you in the BH army, what place? What function and post?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You can switch your microphone on, please, General.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I was able to understand, you're asking me what function I performed before. I was the chief of staff in the command of the 1st Corps in the city of Sarajevo. As chief of staff, I also had the task of territorial defence in Sarajevo and to reorient it, that is to say, to turn it into the armed forces of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you, quite obviously, were a high ranking officer of the BH army. Tell us, please, in the JNA, which rank did you have when you came to the BH army?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: From the BH army, I was lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you see yourself as an officer of the BH army and before as an officer of the JNA? Are you exclusively a military man, a soldier, or were you both a soldier and a politician? How do you view yourself?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Before and today, I see myself as a soldier. I have always been that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To be a soldier, as you understood it, does that mean that you can meddle in political decisions? Can you influence political decisions, decisions made by politicians, or as a soldier, do you execute the orders of the higher command? How do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: As a soldier, it is not my business to meddle in the decisions of the official politicians. It is my duty, as a soldier, if decisions are outside the law, outside the constitution, that the civilian leader and politician be cautioned of that, and it is up to me not to carry things of that kind out, not to implement them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, which decisions you're going to implement or not, that is, decisions made by the politicians, do you assess that yourself and do you consider that to be within the constitutional conduct of a military man?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is, according to the constitution, the professional conduct of a soldier, that is to say, if a politician makes a decision which is not in line with the constitution and orders me to carry that decision out, then as a professional, I am duty-bound to say that it is not in conformity with the constitution and is a violation of other laws, for example, international ones, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Izetbegovic signed the Vance-Owen Plan and, within that framework, the attachment of the BH army in Provinces 10 and 8 to the HVO and vice versa, the HVO in Provinces 9 and 5. Was that rejected by the BH army? Was it contrary to the constitution? What is your opinion on that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Attachment and a decision on that was never signed. In the document of the Vance-Owen Plan, it's stated that there should be a joint withdrawal into these provinces of the military effectives, and the order on attachment emanated from the structure of the HVO and not President Izetbegovic. Before that, there was a law in force, I have a copy of that law on defence, which states what precisely the structure of the BH army was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are going to read something in relation to this, we are going to read a document, but before that, the law on the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who passed it and when? The representatives of the Croat people, did they vote for it? Did the representatives of the Serb people vote for it? Perhaps you didn't understand this as a question. I actually put a question. When was the law on national defence passed, in which year, and did the representatives of all three peoples take part in this? We don't need a date, just approximately.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I again have a look at the documents I have here with me so that I would be as accurate as possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, do so.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I have here a copy of the decree with the force of a law on taking over the law on armed forces and its application in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a republican law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. Just tell me which year this was.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me have a look. The 15th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are not going to go into all of that now. I'm interested in something else. What do you think? If, according to the Vance-Owen Plan, an international agreement that was signed, at least in part, by the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina, recognises the HVO as one of the components of the armed forces and also puts them into certain provinces, does this give legality to the HVO? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I wish to answer this question on the basis of a document, yet again. The armed forces of the republic consist of, I'm reading the law on the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina: "The army of the republic hereinafter 'the army' and also the Croatian Defence Counsel units, as well as other armed forces that are under the unified command of the army --"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, my question was something different.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: The point is that this law says where the HVO belongs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But I'm asking you something else. Would you answer my questions, please, because my time is restricted? Please, could you strictly answer my questions?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think I've finished answering yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I'm a spectator here, as the Court, but if counsel asks the witness a question and the witness wants to answer the question, I think counsel should let the witness answer the question before he goes to his next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This is not always easy to do, not always easy to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Exactly, but he has to answer my question, not move in a different direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The witness answered you. I can sense that your time is limited. I see that you're trying to get to the core of your questions, and I congratulate you for that. Let's not waste any further time, but allow the witness, as we did previously, to familiarise himself with everything, as I did for the Prosecutor. All right. Please continue, and let's not waste any further time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I would like to put a question to you, General. The Vance-Owen Plan establishes that the HVO forces and the BH army forces are being deployed in certain provinces. The Vance-Owen Plan was aware of the situation that the HVO was not part of the BH army, as the national law of Bosnia-Herzegovina had said. Don't you think that an international agreement that was signed by the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina supersedes national legislation, "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: This international agreement was not legally valid yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A new question: Which constitution are you invoking? Which is the constitution that was in force in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992? Could you tell this Court that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I am saying how a military professional, a soldier, is supposed to be behave towards the constitution and towards his state. I have not been dealing with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You're not answering the question, General. Try to answer it. It was more specific than that. Try to focus on the question that's asked. Thank you. Perhaps you could provide the decree that you referred to for the Trial Chamber. If you have one, a copy can be made of it, and it will become an exhibit for the Trial Chamber. But first, concentrate on the specific question that Mr. Nobilo asked you because you haven't answered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I shall repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which was the constitution that was in force in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly which official gazette this was and where this was, but there was a constitution. I don't know whether it was taken over from the previous republic or whether it was corrected. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If it was taken over from the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, who then, according to the constitution, was the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, according to the constitution? According to the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't read this constitution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree that according to the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as an integral part of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the JNA was the only legal armed force, that is to say, the army of that state was the JNA? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that, but I don't know whether that law was taken over or whether it was changed. I don't know. I never read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were not involved in politics, not during this war, not while you were a JNA officer. However, you completed high party schools of the former communist government; is that correct? And you were educated in Marxist doctrine; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: It is correct that I was in the high party school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Kumrovec?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Kumrovec.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can we please have this document distributed and then let's go on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that the usher is very busy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps we can move ahead and just leave these documents aside and let's go on because we're in quite a hurry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, a few words about the fall of Jajce. Can you tell us who gave you this information that the Croats had sold Jajce, that they had handed it over to the Serbs without any fighting? Who said that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I did not say that the Croats handed it over. At the time of the fall of Jajce, I was getting out of Sarajevo, I was travelling, and I received orders to go towards Travnik to see what could be done so that more territory would not fall. The people who had fled were saying that, and they were saying very derogatory things about this matter. That is what I heard from the masses that were passing by, and I compare this to the current situation in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In such situations, is it often the case that people say "They've sold us down the river"? And didn't you hear things like that on all sides in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: No, there were other cases as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, in Kiseljak, that the Territorial Defence was expelled from Kiseljak while Blaskic was there. Can you say specifically whether the Territorial Defence was expelled from Kiseljak before August 1992 or after August 1992?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was expelled before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to show you Defence document D132. We're not going to read the document. It has already been tendered and everybody is familiar with it. You can read it, though. This is an order of the commander of the supreme command of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Sefer Halilovic, and he is writing to the commander of the municipal defence of Kiseljak. He is sending an order on the 8th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: And where was this staff? In Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You think that the order went to Kiseljak and that the staff was not in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I think. There were other staffs that were deployed elsewhere, outside their own territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be logical then to say that this was a forward command post or deployed elsewhere or redeployed, whatever?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: No. They were kicked out, expelled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you think that the civilians, the population of Kiseljak, were expelled from Kiseljak in 1992, or do you think that this pertains only to the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: And quite a bit of the civilian population, the majority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be surprised if you heard that we heard quite a few Bosniaks from Kiseljak here, that before April and notably June, nobody had been expelled? Would you be surprised if you heard that? In 1993.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us one village where Bosniaks were expelled from in Kiseljak in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I do not have specific data about Kiseljak because I was not involved in Kiseljak, and while I was commander of the 3rd Corps, Kiseljak was not related there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one point this morning, you said that you did not understand -- of course, I cannot quote you exactly but I can interpret what you were saying -- that you did not understand why Kiseljak, which was under HVO control, took part in the blockade of Sarajevo. Do you remember having said something to that effect? Well, then I'm asking you the following: Where was the HVO of Kiseljak in touch with the defenders of Sarajevo so that it could take part in the blockade of Sarajevo? Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: The HVO of Kiseljak was together with the Chetniks in the area between Kiseljak and Sarajevo. They never wanted to carry out combat operations together with us vis-à-vis Sarajevo, that is to say, via Kobiljaca. Secondly, they created problems from Hadzici, conditionally speaking -- it's really Tarcin and Pazaric -- to pass via Fojnica to Kiseljak towards Central Bosnia and Visoko, and then people had to go elsewhere, roundabout, because they could not pass this way. So, in fact, in my estimate, they took part in the blockade. Perhaps I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to put the question very precisely, did the HVO of Kiseljak have a front line with the defenders of Sarajevo? Were they in touch? Were they facing them? Did they have territorial contact with the territory that was defended by the defenders of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to answer with a counter-question. On the other side, from Sarajevo, in the region of Stup, in the area facing Kiseljak, that is where an HVO unit was. Why did they not establish contact? So physically they did not have contact. But with the defenders of Sarajevo, this could have been done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did I understand you correctly, that the HVO of Kiseljak did not have physical contact with the defenders of Sarajevo; is that what you said just now? Territorial, physical contact?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that between the HVO of Kiseljak and the defenders of Sarajevo, there was the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly that the key question of cooperation or differences between the HVO and the BH army in the first part of 1992 and possibly afterwards was to agree on the deblockade of Sarajevo or, rather, that the HVO did not agree to that? Was this a key point for you in terms of the differences between you and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: The beginning of '92?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All of 1992. Was this the key issue for you personally and in relation to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not make any decisions to that effect and I did not plan such matters. I personally did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, did you suggest this to the HVO, that you deblockade Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I am telling you, I did not take part in such a plan. Other commands did. And probably the staff of the supreme command. I personally did not. I shall be lying if I tell you anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, this morning you said that you proposed to Blaskic that you go and deblockade Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: But on this side, when I came here to be the commander of the corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, well, that's what I am saying, when you came in 1992 to command the corps.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that we participate in this and that he help and that we take part in it together, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But this is January 1993. That is not 1992. Or the end of December, something like that.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: And you were asking me about the beginning of 1992. In the beginning of 1992, I did not take part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I shall be more specific. I was referring to all of 1992. When you became commander of the 3rd Corps and onwards, was this a point of contention between you and the HVO, their refusal to go and deblockade Sarajevo or, rather, was it your wish to have this carried out?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: This was not a special point of contention but this is what we wanted. We wanted to act together. When I'm saying "we," I'm talking about the 3rd Corps and the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, because I got out of Sarajevo and I know exactly what the people in Sarajevo were experiencing, how they died and how they were famished, and that is why I suggested that we move on this together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now tell the Court: Ever, until the end of the war, was Sarajevo deblockaded by the force of arms, ever? Or was this done by way of an agreement?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: No, but it could have been done had there not been obstacles. That is my assessment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about this encirclement of Sarajevo; was this a professional military siege, encirclement?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a lot of casualties when you attempted the deblockade of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what the fatalities were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, just give me an estimate: small, medium, large?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: There were casualties, but it is relative, what is small and what is big. There were greater casualties because we did not have anything to act with. We did not have anything to act with, and we could not obtain what we needed because others were in the way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now we are going back to January, February 1992 [as interpreted]. You told us here about the joint orders that you made with Blaskic in Kakanj on the 13th of February, 1993 -- and the transcript says February '92 but it's supposed to say February 1993. So we have several joint orders that you presented to us here and that we are going to read because they are now part of the evidence. Tell us, why was it necessary to negotiate? What happened before the 13th of February, 1993? You didn't tell us a thing about the conflict between the HVO and the BH army in Busovaca in January 1993. What is it that happened there in January 1993? Can you tell us about that in a few sentences, please?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: The conflict in Busovaca was not only in January 1993, it began in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any conflict on the 6th?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: The Bosniaks were expelled to Kacuni and the Croats remained in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the Croats expelled from any villages perhaps, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't believe they were expelled, but I do believe that somebody fled because there were conflicts, because there was shooting going on. But that the intention was to expel anybody, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any Croatian houses burned, possibly? What do you think about that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: You're asking me questions and, Mr. President, I have to answer them in the following way: Just as if I was the commander of a platoon there, I was the commander of a corps, and that is very small tactics, but I cannot keep everything in my head. Quite possibly there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, 400 houses, that is small-scale tactics, is it, when you set fire to them and several hundred people are ethnically cleansed from the Kacuni-Bilalovac area, the Croats disappeared? Is that petty tactics? What do you think about that, General?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the conflict in January 1993. You know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: That wasn't then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me help you then, and D450, the document, would it be -- could it be shown, please? D98? May I have D98 first, please, and we'll try to work with that document first. Take a look at these documents, General, please. For example, in document 98, you will see a list of villages and the heads of households, the owners of the houses that were destroyed and burned. They're different places, Kacuni, Nezirovici, Zirovici, Poculica, Bukovci, Kula, Prosije, Gusti Grab --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, which is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel. We were pulling 98.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Would you make it clear what document we're talking about, please, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I'm now looking at document D450/98, so it's "/98."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then we come to the village of Bakije, Jelinak, Putis, Kovacevac, I'm not going to go on reading, but they are lists, as you can see from the other documents as well, of the individuals whose houses were burnt, and in all those villages, there were no more Croats. Did anybody inform you about that? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, these are documents dating to 1996 and 1997 that somebody had compiled and made lists of. They do not date from 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The witnesses spoke about that, sir. I'm asking you whether you know that, in January, these villages were burnt and the Croats expelled?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And ought you to know about that, or do you consider, in view of your position, that you don't have to know about that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm saying that I consider that that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General, I didn't understand. The interpretation I got was that it's not right. What, that the villages were burned or that you should have known? Could you make your answer clearer for us, please.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: It is not true that in 1992 and 1993, January 1993, that these villages were burnt then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I'm going to ask you the following question: Tell us, please, when you issued these joint orders, we have the return of the population, we speak about checkpoints, we speak about limitations to the free passage, did this exist in the BH army and in the HVO or only in the HVO? Did phenomena of this kind exist? Were these things taking place?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the army as well, but at certain regular points which led up to the front line, and to the rear, for the most part, that was the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you didn't hear about the villages that I enumerated. Did you hear about the first crime that was committed in the area of Central Bosnia, about Dusina, the village of Dusina, Lasva, where people had been taken prisoner and where a woman who viewed that, whose husband was killed and his heart pulled out, that it was the HVO soldiers that were taken prisoner and killed and civilians taken prisoner and killed? I'm sure you know where the village is, that is to say, in the territory under your control. Did you hear about that event that took place in January 1993, about the 23rd of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: In January 1993, there were certain groups in existence still which did not enter the structure of the BH army, because the process of forming corps took three to four months, and as the brigades grew, so the reports were sent out that, one by one, the brigades were set up, and as to the alleged crime in Dusina, I do not know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear about the crime, from that day to the present?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: This alleged crime in Dusina was mentioned by the HVO, but I don't know, I did not order or command anything of that kind, any crime of that kind to take place, and I don't want to feel as if I am the accused here by the way the questions are being posed, if possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm speaking about crimes. I did not consider that the commander of the 3rd Corps had ordered anything in this regard, and if you understood it that way, then I apologise. I'm just speaking about crimes and whether you heard about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No. There was no ambiguity here on this point, General. On the part of counsel, there was absolutely no desire to do that, but the Defence can ask whether, in respect of other crimes that were committed, including Ahmici, you might have heard about what had happened. That's how the question should be interpreted. That's how I interpreted it. Please continue, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago, I don't know if you really wanted to say that, you said that up to the present day, you heard about the crime in Dusina by the HVO or the BH army?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't mention the HVO. I didn't mention anybody. I said that there were rumours about the crime in Dusina, but I don't know who perpetrated it, nor did I order it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The husband of the woman, that is to say, she said that this was done by the 7th Muslim Brigade and that she said that it was done by Serif Patkovic who, at the time, was an officer in the 7th Muslim Brigade and that she recognised him on a photograph. What do you have to say to that? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. That kind of thing was never planned or ordered or, indeed, possible. I don't believe it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you ask at joint meetings? Were there any comments with regard to burnt villages between Bilalovac and Kacuni in Dusina? Did you bring anybody to justice? Did you conduct an investigation?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Why should I conduct an investigation? Because I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I agree. I'm now going to read you a document, 732. It is a document dated the 1st of February, 1993. You submitted it today as evidence, and I'd like to read something under point 4, the one but last section above your own signature, where you are ordering your own forces "to prevent the members of the BH army to loot and pilfer and burn, and the protagonists should be detained and brought to justice immediately. For the implementation of this assignment, I make responsible the commanders of the brigades and staff." General, if soldiers under your command did not loot and pilfer and burn, because it is forbidden by law, why then do you have to write this down in an order? If they did not do that, what prompted you to write an order of this kind?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: In war, there are always people that make use of war for their own ends, and there is profiteering and looting, and then they say that was done by the army, the soldiers. To prevent that from taking place, I just issued a warning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there no such instances before this order was compiled?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: The army is also accused of doing things like that, whereas it is the profiteers that make use of the situation, and I felt duty-bound to issue this warning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we understand you, and you must be commended, but were you prompted by incidents of this kind or were there no incidents of this kind and you took this measure to prevent them from occurring?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to answer you a third time?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please, because I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: As I say, in every war, just as in this one, there were profiteers who did things like that. There were those who looted convoys of the UNHCR, for example, and didn't belong to any military formation whatsoever, just to take the goods, seize the goods, to engage in black marketeering, and so on, and I just cautioned that this must not be done by any member of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us move forward then, General. At the negotiations of the 13th of February, 1993, you negotiated with Colonel Blaskic. How did you find him? Was a commander in control of the situation, sovereignly in command of his units, or not? At those negotiations, what was your opinion of him?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic was a very balanced man, a highly built-up professional man, and very precise and detailed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you consider him to be a person of relevance with whom you could negotiate and achieve a peace agreement?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was not able to assess individuals representing the HVO with whom to sign an agreement. He was the representative of the HVO, and that is how my relationship was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had no comments?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: D188 is the next exhibit that we would like to discuss, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, would you read this document, acquaint yourself with it, and I am going to read out just one sentence from the document in a minute or two. This is your document, a document of the 3rd Corps, dated the 12th of February, 1993, where you, in the second paragraph, state the following, and in the English text, it is the third paragraph, in fact. You say: "We assume that Colonel Tihomir Blaskic is isolated in Kiseljak and that his readiness to resolve the problems is a lie, that somebody else is solving the problems instead of Tiho Blaskic and that there is no point in negotiating as whatever is agreed upon will not have any result." General, did you write that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you then alter what you said before the Tribunal, and can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the 12th of February. This is a concrete meeting at which this occurred when Mr. -- I can't find his name and surname. Just one moment, please. The document was signed by an unauthorised person, in our view, and it was our assumption that at that meeting, at that particular time, Tiho was isolated in Kiseljak, and in the previous statement, I speak about our other meetings and the following meetings and how I experienced him during those meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If he was isolated in Kiseljak, who then commanded, in Busovaca, the troops that were fighting there?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. President. That is my assumption. It need not be a correct assumption.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but what did you base your assumption on?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I say this because the number two man signed the document, not Tihomir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So who signed the document, General?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The situation that Blaskic was isolated in Kiseljak, what did you assume, that he was not master of the situation in Kiseljak? Was that the essential point?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to read through this document slowly. You just read out one paragraph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We don't have much time, so we have to move forward. I have one more question that I want to ask you. Did you consider that Blaskic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say that you're withdrawing your question, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No, no, Mr. President, I just asked the questions I asked, but I said that I'd like to move forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I heard in the answer that the witness doesn't have the time to read the document. Is it a long document? Because we don't have the English version on the ELMO. What would you prefer to do, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have obtained an answer, we're satisfied with the answer, and we'd like to move forward because our time is limited, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We're going to take a break at a quarter after four, and we will resume at 4.35, and then you can finish around 5.00, which means that you have about 35 more minutes, unless you're like Mr. Kehoe and you finish earlier. That would be another problem. You have the right to use all your time, Mr. Nobilo. Proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We'll see how things proceed and whether we'll be able to end before time. Why not?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said this morning, General, that the 3rd Corps had 32.000 soldiers and that a third was armed. Do you maintain that now?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time was that? Can we be more specific?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: I should like to remind you that I was commander of the corps from the end of 1992 up until October or November of 1993, and I'm speaking about that time and in that name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if my calculations are correct, a third of 32.000 is about 10.300 -- 10.600, 10.700 soldiers under arms; is that it?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at the front line, a big front line, a big number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The front line, you said, was 500 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: A lot of time has gone by, Mr. President, and I apologise, so I can't remember everything. I'm just seeking confirmation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we said a third, did we?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, that is what you said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, you said this morning that in Vitez and in the villages around Vitez, there were no military formations, and you used the term "military effectives." Is that correct? Before the open conflict, the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there were not. We can understand your answer in two ways. Are you saying that there were no military effectives in the villages around Vitez before the conflict of the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Furthermore, you said that in Stari Vitez, the civilians found themselves in an encirclement, from the 16th of April onwards, 1993. Do you maintain that now still?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: Civilians in an encirclement?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that is what you said this morning.
